title: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
summary: Exfiltration over an alternative protocol covers theft in which the data leaves through a protocol other than the one carrying the command and control channel, and often to a different network destination than the main control server. The point is resilience: if the operator's control channel is a narrow or well-profiled connection, a separate high-volume channel over File Transfer Protocol (FTP), mail, web, Domain Name System (DNS), or file sharing moves the data without disturbing it, and blocks on the control channel do not stop the theft. The data is first staged, usually compressed and sometimes encrypted or encoded, then pushed out with tooling already present on the host, such as command line file transfer clients, scripted web requests, or built-in cloud and software-as-a-service download and upload interfaces. The sub-techniques separate the channel by how the payload is protected: symmetric encryption with a shared secret, asymmetric encryption with a public key, or no encryption at all with obfuscation instead. Detection focuses on the shape of the traffic rather than the protocol: unusual outbound volume from a workstation or server, a host contacting a destination it never used before, transfers outside business hours, large uploads to file sharing or code hosting services, and rare protocols appearing on a network that normally carries only web traffic. Legitimate backups, software updates, and cloud synchronisation produce similar volumes, so identification relies on matching the destination and the account against expectations.

beginner.definition: This is stealing data by sending it out through a different channel than the one the attacker uses to control the victim machine. Common channels are file transfer, email, web requests or domain name lookups. The data usually goes to a different place than the control traffic.
beginner.whyItMatters: If defenders block one channel, the theft can continue on another. The data often travels over protocols your network must keep open to work. Because the same tools are used for real business, a single blocked connection may not look alarming. Losing the data matters more than losing control of the machine.
howItWorks: The attacker gathers files on the victim machine and places them in one staging folder.
The files are compressed, and often encrypted or encoded so the contents are unreadable.
A transfer tool that is already on the machine is used, so nothing unusual is installed.
The data is sent over a protocol that is not the main control channel, to a separate server.
Transfers may be split into smaller pieces or spread over time to stay under volume limits.
Cloud services can also be used, with the data uploaded through their normal interfaces.
beginner.example: Imagine a post office where all parcels are checked at the main desk. A thief inside decides not to post parcels there at all. Instead they walk to the newsagent next door and send the goods as ordinary letters, a few at a time. The main desk sees nothing unusual, because the theft never passes through it.
takeaways: Exfiltration can use any protocol the network allows, not just the control channel.
Look at traffic volume and destination, because the protocol itself is often normal.
Know which servers and services in your estate are allowed to send data outward.

objectives: Explain why an adversary would exfiltrate over a protocol separate from the command and control channel.
Describe how data is staged, prepared and transferred during alternative protocol exfiltration.
List common protocols and built-in utilities that can carry the stolen data.
Identify detection approaches based on volume, destination and timing rather than protocol alone.
Compare the encrypted and unencrypted variants of this technique and their observable differences.
